title: Passé composé or imparfait
description: Tell a past story, choosing between background and events.

guide.summary: Telling a past story in French needs two tenses at once: the imparfait paints the scene and what was going on, the passé composé reports what happened. This page shows how to decide, verb by verb.

sections.title: Building the two tenses
sections.text: The imparfait is one word: take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add the endings. The passé composé is two words: avoir or être in the present, plus the past participle.
steps: Imparfait: nous dormons gives dorm-, then -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
Passé composé: choose avoir or être, put it in the present, then add the participle.
Movement and reflexive verbs (aller, partir, rester, rentrer, s’ouvrir) take être, and their participle agrees with the subject.
Être and avoir are irregular: j’étais, j’avais; their participles are été and eu.

examples.fr: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

examples.fr: Nous sommes allés à la plage.

watch: Je becomes j’ before a vowel: j’ai entendu, never je ai entendu.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject: nous avons attendu, not nous avons attendus.
-ais, -ait and -aient sound alike; only the subject tells you which one to write.

sections.title: Which tense? Ask what the verb answers
sections.text: Every past verb answers one of these questions. Ask it verb by verb, not once for the whole sentence.

rows: j’ai habité à Lyon deux ans

steps: Find every past verb in the sentence.
Ask the question above for each one on its own: most stories need both tenses.
Let the time words (soudain, d’habitude, pendant deux ans) settle any doubt.

examples.fr: D’habitude, il prenait le bus, mais ce jour-là, il a pris un taxi.
examples.en: He usually took the bus, but that day he took a taxi.

watch: Do not pick one tense for the whole sentence: a story mixes them.
English “was” is not always the imparfait: “I was scared when I saw it” starts at one moment.

sections.title: Scene or event?
sections.text: A story has a stage and things that happen on it. The stage is imparfait; the events are passé composé.

rows: the next step in the story

steps: Put weather, places, moods and anything already under way in the imparfait.
Put each step that moves the story forward in the passé composé.
Two descriptions side by side are both imparfait; two events in a row are both passé composé.

examples.fr: Il faisait froid, alors je suis rentré tôt.
examples.en: It was cold, so I went home early.

watch: Encore, toujours and déjà with an action still running point to the imparfait.
Alors and donc introduce what you did next: that is an event, not a description.

sections.title: One action cut short by another
sections.text: When something happens in the middle of something else, the two verbs take different tenses.

rows: the short event that breaks in
pendant que tu faisais la vaisselle

steps: Say it in English: the “was …-ing” verb goes in the imparfait.
The verb you could put after “and then” goes in the passé composé.
Quand usually introduces the event; the verb right after pendant que stays background.

examples.fr: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

examples.fr: Pendant que je lisais, elle écrivait.
examples.en: While I was reading, she was writing.

watch: Both verbs in the passé composé gives two events in a row, not an interruption.
Both in the imparfait removes the event: nothing happens any more.

sections.title: Habit or one occasion?
sections.text: The imparfait is the tense of “used to” and “would always”. The passé composé is for the one time it was different.
steps: Find the time expression and decide: repeated, or one occasion?
Repeated, or a whole period of life, means imparfait.
One named occasion means passé composé, even inside a sentence about habits.

examples.fr: Tous les étés, nous allions en Bretagne.
examples.en: Every summer we used to go to Brittany.

examples.fr: Ce jour-là, elle a pris le train.
examples.en: That day she took the train.

watch: Le mercredi means every Wednesday; mercredi dernier means one single Wednesday.
The habit half and the exception half of one sentence take different tenses.

sections.title: How long did it last?
sections.text: A length of time that is stated and finished makes the action a whole block, so it takes the passé composé — even when the verb describes a state.

rows: il a travaillé ici pendant deux ans
a state with a stated length
ils ont été malades une semaine
il travaillait ici à cette époque

steps: Look for pendant, or a length on its own: deux ans, quarante minutes, toute la nuit.
If that length is over, use the passé composé, whatever the verb means.
With no length given, a state or a setting stays in the imparfait.
Then check the auxiliary and, with être, the agreement of the participle.

examples.fr: J’ai habité à Lyon pendant deux ans.
examples.en: I lived in Lyon for two years.

examples.fr: Il habitait à Lyon quand je l’ai connu.
examples.en: He was living in Lyon when I met him.

watch: Pendant closes a finished period; depuis keeps a state open and behaves differently.
Être, avoir and habiter follow this rule too: a counted period turns them into events.

sections.title: A feeling: already there, or starting now?
sections.text: The same feeling takes either tense. What decides is the moment it began.

rows: elle a eu froid en sortant
il a eu honte quand tout le monde a ri

steps: Ask when the feeling or the state began.
Already there, lasting, part of the description: imparfait.
Arriving at a precise moment, as a reaction: passé composé.
Use avoir with peur, faim, soif, froid, chaud, honte — never être.

examples.fr: J’avais peur du noir quand j’étais petit.
examples.en: I was afraid of the dark when I was little.

examples.fr: J’ai eu peur quand j’ai entendu le bruit.
examples.en: I got scared when I heard the noise.

watch: English “was afraid” covers both; only the starting moment decides.

sections.title: Words that decide the tense for you
sections.text: Some time expressions settle the question on their own. Learn them as two lists.
steps: Scan for a time expression before you choose the tense.
One-moment words take the passé composé; repetition and period words take the imparfait.
The verb right after pendant que is always background: imparfait.

examples.fr: À cette époque, je travaillais à Paris.
examples.en: Back then I was working in Paris.

watch: Une fois means once and takes the passé composé; parfois means sometimes and takes the imparfait.
Ce jour-là is one day; à cette époque is a whole period.

steps: Ask what the verb does: set the scene, or tell what happened?
Weather, places, moods and anything still under way: imparfait.
A finished step that moves the story on: passé composé.
With the passé composé, check the auxiliary: aller, partir, rester and rentrer take être.
Find the two verbs and ask which one was already under way.
The “was …-ing” one goes in the imparfait.
The one that happens at a point, usually after quand, goes in the passé composé.
After pendant que, the action runs alongside: imparfait.
Read the time expression: again and again, or that one time?
D’habitude, souvent, tous les…, le lundi, quand j’étais petit: imparfait.
Un jour, un été, ce jour-là, une fois: passé composé.
Then check the ending for the person, and the auxiliary if you need one.
Look for a measured length: pendant deux ans, quarante minutes, toute la soirée.
A finished length makes it a whole block: passé composé, even for a state verb.
No length given means you are just describing: imparfait.
Build the passé composé with the right auxiliary and watch the participle agreement.
Ask when the feeling or the state began.
Already there and lasting: imparfait. Starting at that moment, as a reaction: passé composé.
Keep avoir with peur, faim, froid, chaud; être never goes with them.
Spot the time expression first.
Soudain, tout à coup, une fois, ce jour-là: one moment, so passé composé.
Chaque jour, souvent, à cette époque and the verb after pendant que: imparfait.
Then conjugate: imparfait endings on the nous stem, or auxiliary plus participle.

exercises.source: Samedi dernier, il faisait beau, alors nous ____ à la plage et nous avons nagé.
exercises.hint: Going to the beach is one of the events of that Saturday, like the swimming.
exercises.feedback: The weather is background, but what you did next moves the story on.
exercises.explanation: Il faisait beau is the background. Going to the beach is a completed event in a sequence, so it takes the passé composé with être: nous sommes allés.

mistakes.why: Allions is the imparfait, which would turn the beach trip into a background situation or a habit. Here it is one of the things you did that Saturday, just like nous avons nagé.
Aller never takes avoir in the passé composé: it takes être, and the participle then agrees with the subject.

exercises.row: the next step in the story

exercises.source: Quand je suis arrivé à la fête, les invités dansaient et la musique ____ très forte.
exercises.hint: What did the party look like when I arrived?
exercises.feedback: The music is part of the scene, like the dancing guests.
exercises.explanation: The scene I found on arrival is background, so it takes the imparfait: la musique était très forte.

mistakes.why: A été presents the loud music as a completed event with a start and an end. Here it is part of the scene you walked into, described alongside les invités dansaient.
Est is the present. The rest of the sentence is past (je suis arrivé, dansaient), so a present form cannot fit.

exercises.instruction: Write pleuvoir in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Quand nous sommes sortis, le ciel était gris et il ____ (pleuvoir) encore.
exercises.hint: Encore means the rain was still going on.
exercises.feedback: This is part of the scene, not a new event.
exercises.explanation: The rain was still in progress when we went out, so it is background: il pleuvait.

mistakes.why: A plu makes the rain a finished event, but encore says it had not stopped: it was still falling as you went out.
Pleut is the present, and the whole scene is past (nous sommes sortis, le ciel était gris).
Those are the je/tu and ils/elles endings. Weather verbs have only the impersonal il as subject, so they take the il ending.

exercises.source: It was cold, so she stayed at home.
answers: Il faisait froid, alors elle est restée à la maison.
Il faisait froid, donc elle est restée à la maison.
Il faisait froid, alors elle est restée chez elle.
Il faisait froid, donc elle est restée chez elle.
Il faisait froid, elle est donc restée à la maison.
Il faisait froid, elle est donc restée chez elle.
exercises.hint: The weather is the background; staying at home is what she did.
exercises.feedback: Use one tense for the situation and another for the event.
exercises.explanation: Il faisait froid describes the situation (imparfait). Elle est restée is the completed event (passé composé with être, restée agreeing with elle).

answers: Il a fait froid, alors elle est restée à la maison.
mistakes.why: A fait froid presents the cold as one finished event. Here the cold is the situation that explains her decision, so it belongs in the describing tense.

answers: Il faisait froid, alors elle restait à la maison.
mistakes.why: Restait makes staying at home a habit or an ongoing state. It was one decision on one day, so it needs the tense for completed events.

answers: Il faisait froid, alors elle a resté à la maison.
mistakes.why: Rester takes être in the passé composé, not avoir, and its participle then agrees with elle.

answers: Il était froid, alors elle est restée à la maison.
mistakes.why: Il était froid would mean that some masculine thing felt cold to the touch. Weather uses faire: il faisait froid.

exercises.source: The house was empty when I (masculine) got home.
answers: La maison était vide quand je suis rentré.
exercises.hint: One verb describes, the other tells what happened.
exercises.feedback: The state of the house is background.
exercises.explanation: The empty house is description (était); getting home is the event (je suis rentré).

answers: La maison a été vide quand je suis rentré.
mistakes.why: A été vide turns the empty house into an event that happened and ended. The empty house is the scene you walked into, so it is a description.

exercises.source: Quand je suis rentrée, les rues ont été vides.
answers: Quand je suis rentrée, les rues étaient vides.
exercises.hint: Which verb describes the scene?
exercises.feedback: The empty streets are not an event.
exercises.explanation: The streets being empty is a description, so it takes the imparfait: les rues étaient vides.

answers: Quand je suis rentrée, les rues ont été vides.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Ont été vides makes the empty streets an event, but they are the scene you came home to.

answers: Quand je rentrais, les rues étaient vides.
mistakes.why: This changes the wrong verb: coming home happened at one moment and is the event the sentence is built on.

answers: Quand j’étais rentrée, les rues étaient vides.
mistakes.why: Étais rentrée is a different tense again, used for what had happened before something else. Only one verb in this sentence needed fixing, and it was not that one.

exercises.instruction: Tell this in the past, as something that happened yesterday.
exercises.source: La boulangerie est fermée, alors nous achetons du pain au supermarché.
answers: La boulangerie était fermée, alors nous avons acheté du pain au supermarché.
exercises.hint: One verb describes the situation, the other is what you did.
exercises.feedback: The closed bakery and the buying do not take the same tense.
exercises.explanation: The closed bakery is the situation (la boulangerie était fermée); buying bread is the completed event (nous avons acheté).

answers: La boulangerie a été fermée, alors nous avons acheté du pain au supermarché.
mistakes.why: A été fermée reports the closing as an event. The closed bakery is the situation that explains the trip to the supermarket.

answers: La boulangerie était fermée, alors nous achetions du pain au supermarché.
mistakes.why: Achetions makes the shopping a habit or an action in progress, but buying the bread is the one thing that happened.

answers: La boulangerie était fermée, alors nous achetons du pain au supermarché.
mistakes.why: Only the first verb moved into the past: achetons is still the present, and the whole sentence is about yesterday.

exercises.source: Je ____ quand le téléphone a sonné.
exercises.hint: What was going on when the phone rang?
exercises.feedback: The phone ringing interrupted something that was already in progress.
exercises.explanation: An action in progress when another event happens takes the imparfait: je dormais.

mistakes.why: Ai dormi makes the sleep a finished block of time. The phone rang in the middle of it, so the sleeping was still under way.
Dormait carries the il/elle ending. The subject is je, which takes the -ais ending.

exercises.instruction: Write prendre in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Elle ____ (prendre) sa douche quand quelqu’un a frappé à la porte, alors elle n’a pas ouvert.
exercises.hint: The knock came in the middle of something, and she could not answer.
exercises.feedback: The shower was already going on.
exercises.explanation: The shower was in progress and the knock interrupted it: elle prenait sa douche.

mistakes.why: A pris makes the shower one finished event. The knock came while she was in it, which is why she could not open the door.
Prend is the present, but the sentence is a past story (a frappé, n’a pas ouvert).
Those are the je/tu and ils/elles endings. Elle is one person and takes the il/elle ending.

exercises.instruction: Write casser in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Pendant que tu faisais la vaisselle, le chat ____ (casser) un verre.
exercises.hint: Breaking a glass happens in one moment.
exercises.feedback: The washing-up is the background; the cat did something once.
exercises.explanation: Pendant que tu faisais la vaisselle is the ongoing background; the broken glass is a single event: le chat a cassé un verre.

mistakes.why: Cassait would describe the breaking as lasting or repeated. Breaking a glass takes one instant, and it is what happened during the washing-up.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the word that follows it, so the -e is wrong here.
Casser takes avoir in the passé composé; est cassé would describe a glass that is broken, not the cat breaking it.

exercises.row: the short event that breaks in

exercises.source: I was reading when he arrived.
answers: Je lisais quand il est arrivé.
J’étais en train de lire quand il est arrivé.
J’étais en train de lire lorsqu’il est arrivé.
Quand il est arrivé, je lisais.
Quand il est arrivé, j’étais en train de lire.
Lorsqu’il est arrivé, j’étais en train de lire.
exercises.hint: One action was in progress; the other interrupted it.
exercises.feedback: Was reading and arrived do not take the same tense.
exercises.explanation: The reading was in progress (je lisais); his arrival is the interrupting event (il est arrivé).

answers: J’ai lu quand il est arrivé.
mistakes.why: J’ai lu presents the reading as a finished block. His arrival cut into it, so the reading was still going on.
Arrivait turns his arrival into background too. Arriving happens at one moment: it is the event that interrupts.

answers: Je lisais quand il a arrivé.
mistakes.why: Arriver takes être in the passé composé, never avoir.

exercises.source: They were eating when the storm started.
answers: Ils mangeaient quand l’orage a commencé.
exercises.hint: One action was going on; the storm started at one moment.
exercises.feedback: Use one tense for the meal and the other for the storm.
exercises.explanation: The meal was in progress (ils mangeaient); the storm starting is the event (l’orage a commencé).

answers: Ils ont mangé quand l’orage a commencé.
mistakes.why: Ont mangé makes the meal a finished block, so nothing is left for the storm to interrupt.
Commençait puts the storm in the background as well. A storm breaking out is a single moment.

answers: Ils ont mangé quand l’orage commençait.
mistakes.why: This swaps the two roles: the meal is what was under way, and the storm starting is the moment that cut into it.

exercises.source: Je traversais la rue quand je voyais un accident.
answers: Je traversais la rue quand j’ai vu un accident.
exercises.hint: Which action interrupted the other?
exercises.feedback: Seeing the accident happened at one moment.
exercises.explanation: Crossing the street was in progress (imparfait); seeing the accident is the event that happened (passé composé): j’ai vu.

answers: Je traversais la rue quand je voyais un accident.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Voyais describes seeing as something ongoing, but you caught sight of the accident at one point.

answers: J’ai traversé la rue quand je voyais un accident.
mistakes.why: This changes the wrong verb: crossing the street was the action in progress, and the second verb is still untouched.

answers: J’ai traversé la rue quand j’ai vu un accident.
mistakes.why: Two events in a row lose the interruption: the crossing was already under way when the accident appeared.

exercises.row: the short event that breaks in

exercises.source: dormir · tu · imparfait
exercises.hint: Start from nous dormons.
exercises.feedback: Use the stem dorm- and the tu ending.
exercises.explanation: Nous dormons gives dorm-, plus -ais: tu dormais, as in tu dormais quand je suis parti.

mistakes.why: That is the il/elle ending. Tu takes the -ais ending in the imparfait.
That is the passé composé, the tense for finished events; the question asks for the tense of an action in progress.
Those are the nous and vous endings, and the subject here is tu.
Dors is the present. The imparfait is built on the nous form of the present, dormons, plus its own endings.

exercises.source: D’habitude, je ____ le bus, mais ce jour-là, j’ai pris un taxi.
exercises.hint: D’habitude tells you how things usually were.
exercises.feedback: The bus was the usual habit; the taxi was the one-time exception.
exercises.explanation: A habit takes the imparfait: d’habitude, je prenais le bus. Ce jour-là, a single occasion, takes the passé composé.

mistakes.why: That form reports one finished event, and the sentence already has one: the taxi ce jour-là. D’habitude is about what happened over and over.
Prenait carries the il/elle ending, but the subject is je.

exercises.source: Tous les étés, nous allions en Bretagne, mais un été, nous ____ en Espagne.
exercises.hint: Un été points to one particular summer.
exercises.feedback: The habit is already given; this verb is the exception.
exercises.explanation: Un été is a single occasion, so it takes the passé composé: nous sommes partis. Partir takes être.

mistakes.why: Partions is the habit tense, the one allions already uses. Un été singles out one summer that broke the habit.
Partir never takes avoir in the passé composé: it takes être, and the participle agrees with the subject.

exercises.instruction: Write aller in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Quand elle était enfant, elle ____ (aller) chez sa grand-mère le mercredi.
exercises.hint: Le mercredi here means every Wednesday.
exercises.feedback: This is something that happened again and again.
exercises.explanation: A repeated childhood habit takes the imparfait: elle allait chez sa grand-mère le mercredi.

mistakes.why: That makes the visit one finished trip, but le mercredi here means every Wednesday, week after week.
Aller takes être in the passé composé, never avoir — and one finished trip is not what le mercredi describes.
Va is the present. The sentence is set in her childhood (quand elle était enfant), so the verb must be past.
That is the ils/elles ending, for several people, and the subject here is one girl.
Allais is the je/tu form. The subject here is elle, which takes the il/elle ending.

exercises.instruction: Write dormir in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: D’habitude, Marc se levait tôt, mais un dimanche, il ____ (dormir) jusqu’à midi.
exercises.hint: Un dimanche is one particular Sunday.
exercises.feedback: The habit is getting up early; this verb is the exception.
exercises.explanation: Un dimanche is a single occasion with a clear end (jusqu’à midi), so it takes the passé composé: il a dormi.

mistakes.why: Dormait is the tense of the habit, and the habit is already given by se levait tôt. Un dimanche points to the one Sunday that broke it.
Dormais carries the je/tu ending of the habit tense, and the subject here is il.
Dormir takes avoir in the passé composé, not être.

exercises.source: One day, I saw a fox.
answers: Un jour, j’ai vu un renard.
J’ai vu un renard un jour.
exercises.hint: Un jour means one particular day.
exercises.feedback: This is a single event, not a habit.
exercises.explanation: Un jour marks a single occasion, so it takes the passé composé: j’ai vu un renard.

answers: Un jour, je voyais un renard.
mistakes.why: Je voyais describes seeing as ongoing or repeated, but un jour points to one single occasion.

answers: Un jour, je vois un renard.
mistakes.why: Je vois is the present, and the sentence tells something that already happened.

answers: Un jour, je suis vu un renard.
mistakes.why: Voir takes avoir in the passé composé, not être.

exercises.source: When I was little, I used to play the piano. (a boy speaking)
answers: Quand j’étais petit, je jouais du piano.
Quand j’étais petit, je faisais du piano.
Lorsque j’étais petit, je jouais du piano.
Lorsque j’étais petit, je faisais du piano.
Je jouais du piano quand j’étais petit.
Je faisais du piano quand j’étais petit.
Je jouais du piano lorsque j’étais petit.
Je faisais du piano lorsque j’étais petit.
exercises.hint: When I was little describes a period; used to play is a habit during it.
exercises.feedback: Neither verb is a single event.
exercises.explanation: Both verbs take the imparfait: j’étais petit is a state, je jouais du piano a habit. Instruments take jouer de (or faire de: je faisais du piano).

answers: Quand j’étais petit, j’ai joué du piano.
mistakes.why: J’ai joué names one finished session at the piano, but “used to play” is a habit that ran through those whole years.

answers: Quand j’ai été petit, je jouais du piano.
mistakes.why: J’ai été petit turns childhood into a single finished event. A period of life you are describing is background.

answers: Quand j’étais petit, je jouais le piano.
mistakes.why: Instruments take jouer de: du piano, de la guitare. Jouer le piano is not French.

answers: Quand j’étais petite, je jouais du piano.
mistakes.why: Petite is the feminine form, but the note says a boy is speaking.

exercises.source: D’habitude, mon père a préparé le dîner.
answers: D’habitude, mon père préparait le dîner.
exercises.hint: What does d’habitude tell you?
exercises.feedback: D’habitude does not go with a single event.
exercises.explanation: D’habitude marks a habit, which takes the imparfait: mon père préparait le dîner.

answers: D’habitude, mon père a préparé le dîner.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. A préparé names one finished dinner, while d’habitude says it happened again and again.

answers: D’habitude, mon père préparais le dîner.
mistakes.why: Préparais carries the je/tu ending, and mon père is he.

answers: Une fois, mon père a préparé le dîner.
mistakes.why: This fixes the time word instead of the verb. The task keeps d’habitude and changes the tense to match it.

exercises.instruction: Turn this into a habit: replace Ce jour-là with D’habitude and change the tense.
exercises.source: Ce jour-là, elle est rentrée à pied.
exercises.hint: A habit needs a different past tense from a single occasion.
exercises.feedback: Change the verb as well as the time expression.
exercises.explanation: D’habitude marks a habit, so the verb goes into the imparfait: elle rentrait à pied.

answers: D’habitude, elle est rentrée à pied.
mistakes.why: The time word changed but the verb did not: a single finished event does not fit d’habitude.
Rentrais carries the je/tu ending, and the subject elle takes the il/elle one.

answers: Ce jour-là, elle rentrait à pied.
mistakes.why: This keeps the old time word. The sentence has to start from d’habitude, which is what makes the verb change.

answers: D’habitude, elle a rentré à pied.
mistakes.why: Rentrer takes être here, not avoir, and a habit is not a single finished event anyway.

exercises.source: Il ____ à Lyon pendant deux ans, puis il est parti à Paris.
exercises.hint: Pendant deux ans gives a finished length of time.
exercises.feedback: A period with a stated, finished duration is seen as a whole.
exercises.explanation: A finished, limited duration takes the passé composé: il a habité à Lyon pendant deux ans. Habiter takes avoir.

mistakes.why: Habitait leaves the stay open, as the setting for something else. Pendant deux ans closes it: the two years are counted and over.
Habiter takes avoir, not être; est habité would mean the place is lived in by someone.

exercises.instruction: Write attendre in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Hier, nous ____ (attendre) le bus pendant quarante minutes.
exercises.hint: The wait had a measured length and it is over.
exercises.feedback: A stated duration makes the action a completed whole.
exercises.explanation: Pendant quarante minutes gives a limited duration, so the passé composé: nous avons attendu.

mistakes.why: Attendions leaves the wait open as background, but pendant quarante minutes measures it from start to finish.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, so the -s is wrong.
Attendre takes avoir in the passé composé, not être.
That is still the infinitive. After the auxiliary you need the past participle.

exercises.source: She slept for ten hours.
answers: Elle a dormi pendant dix heures.
exercises.hint: For ten hours is a finished length of time.
exercises.feedback: A limited duration is not background.
exercises.explanation: A completed, measured duration takes the passé composé: elle a dormi pendant dix heures.

mistakes.why: Dormait describes the sleep as background with no end in sight, but “for ten hours” measures it and closes it.

answers: Elle a dormi pour dix heures.
mistakes.why: Pour is not used for a finished length of time in the past; French uses pendant, or no preposition at all.

answers: Elle est dormie pendant dix heures.
mistakes.why: Dormir takes avoir in the passé composé, not être.

exercises.source: Mes grands-parents étaient mariés pendant cinquante ans.
answers: Mes grands-parents ont été mariés pendant cinquante ans.
exercises.hint: Pendant cinquante ans closes the period.
exercises.feedback: A state with a finished duration is seen as a whole.
exercises.explanation: With pendant and a finished period, even a state takes the passé composé: ils ont été mariés pendant cinquante ans.

answers: Mes grands-parents étaient mariés pendant cinquante ans.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Étaient mariés leaves the marriage open as a description, but pendant cinquante ans counts it out from beginning to end.

answers: Mes grands-parents se sont mariés pendant cinquante ans.
mistakes.why: Se sont mariés means they got married, a one-day event; the sentence is about how long the marriage lasted.

answers: Mes grands-parents étaient mariés depuis cinquante ans.
mistakes.why: Depuis counts up to a later moment and keeps the state open, but this sentence gives a period that is finished, and the verb still needs changing.

exercises.row: a state with a stated length

exercises.source: habiter · nous · passé composé
exercises.hint: Habiter takes avoir.
exercises.feedback: The passé composé needs an auxiliary and a past participle.
exercises.explanation: Nous avons habité, as in nous avons habité à Nice pendant un an.

mistakes.why: Habiter takes avoir, not être.
That is the imparfait, used for an open, undated stay; the question asks for the tense of a finished one.
That is still the infinitive after the auxiliary; the passé composé needs the past participle.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, so the -s is wrong.

exercises.source: We talked for an hour.
answers: Nous avons parlé pendant une heure.
exercises.hint: Pendant une heure gives a finished duration.
exercises.feedback: A conversation with a stated length is a completed whole.
exercises.explanation: A limited duration takes the passé composé: nous avons parlé pendant une heure.

mistakes.why: Parlions leaves the conversation open as background, but the sentence measures it: one hour, from start to finish.

exercises.source: Ils restent en Italie pendant une semaine.
answers: Ils sont restés en Italie pendant une semaine.
exercises.hint: Pendant une semaine gives a finished period.
exercises.feedback: A stated duration takes the tense for completed actions. Rester takes être.
exercises.explanation: A limited duration takes the passé composé: ils sont restés, with restés agreeing with ils.

answers: Ils restaient en Italie pendant une semaine.
mistakes.why: Restaient describes the stay as background with no end, but pendant une semaine gives it a finished length.

answers: Ils ont resté en Italie pendant une semaine.
mistakes.why: Rester takes être in the passé composé, not avoir.

answers: Ils sont resté en Italie pendant une semaine.
mistakes.why: With être the participle agrees with the subject, and ils is plural.

answers: Ils restent en Italie pendant une semaine.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged: restent is still the present, and the task is to move it into the past.

exercises.source: Soudain, elle a vu le serpent et elle ____ peur.
exercises.hint: The fear started at that exact moment.
exercises.feedback: This is not a feeling that was already there.
exercises.explanation: A feeling that begins at a precise moment is an event: elle a eu peur. Être is not used with peur.

mistakes.why: Avait peur would mean the fear was already there before she saw anything. Soudain says it arrived with the snake.
French does not say être peur: fear goes with avoir.

exercises.source: La petite fille ____ peur du noir, alors elle dormait avec la lumière allumée.
exercises.hint: Was this fear a single moment or a lasting state?
exercises.feedback: Her fear of the dark was a lasting situation, like her sleeping habit.
exercises.explanation: A lasting state takes the imparfait: elle avait peur du noir.

mistakes.why: That form marks the moment a fear starts. Her fear of the dark is a lasting trait, which is why she slept with the light on.
Peur goes with avoir, not être: être peur is not French.

exercises.instruction: Write avoir in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Quand la porte a claqué, le bébé ____ (avoir) peur et il a pleuré.
exercises.hint: The fear was caused by the door slamming.
exercises.feedback: The fear began at a precise moment and led to the crying.
exercises.explanation: A state that starts at a given moment takes the passé composé: le bébé a eu peur.

mistakes.why: Avait peur would mean the baby was frightened before the door. The fear came from the slam and led straight to the crying.
Peur goes with avoir, never être.
Eu on its own is only the participle; this tense needs its auxiliary in front of it.

exercises.instruction: Write avoir in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Quand nous habitions à Paris, nous ____ (avoir) un petit appartement.
exercises.hint: Having the flat was a lasting situation during that time.
exercises.feedback: Nothing changed at one moment here.
exercises.explanation: A lasting state during a past period takes the imparfait: nous avions un petit appartement.

mistakes.why: That form marks the moment you got the flat. The sentence describes what your life was like all the while you lived in Paris.
Avait carries the il/elle ending, and the subject is nous.
Avons is the present, but the sentence is past, alongside habitions.

exercises.source: I got scared when I saw the dog.
answers: J’ai eu peur quand j’ai vu le chien.
J’ai eu peur lorsque j’ai vu le chien.
Quand j’ai vu le chien, j’ai eu peur.
Lorsque j’ai vu le chien, j’ai eu peur.
J’ai pris peur quand j’ai vu le chien.
Quand j’ai vu le chien, j’ai pris peur.
exercises.hint: Got scared means the fear started at that moment.
exercises.feedback: A fear that begins is an event.
exercises.explanation: The fear starts when I see the dog, so both verbs take the passé composé: j’ai eu peur, j’ai vu.

answers: J’avais peur quand j’ai vu le chien.
mistakes.why: J’avais peur says the fear was already there before the dog appeared, but “got scared” means it started right then.

answers: J’ai eu peur quand je voyais le chien.
mistakes.why: Je voyais stretches the sighting out as background; catching sight of the dog is the instant that caused the fear.

answers: J’étais peur quand j’ai vu le chien.
mistakes.why: Peur goes with avoir, not être.

exercises.source: Soudain, le chien a aboyé et Léo avait peur.
answers: Soudain, le chien a aboyé et Léo a eu peur.
exercises.hint: When did Léo’s fear start?
exercises.feedback: The fear is a reaction to the barking.
exercises.explanation: The fear begins at that moment, so it is an event: Léo a eu peur.

answers: Soudain, le chien a aboyé et Léo avait peur.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Avait peur puts the fear there before the barking, but soudain makes the bark the trigger.

answers: Soudain, le chien aboyait et Léo avait peur.
mistakes.why: This changes the wrong verb: soudain announces the bark as the event, and the feeling is what still needs fixing.

answers: Soudain, le chien a aboyé et Léo a été peur.
mistakes.why: Peur goes with avoir, never être.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite so the fear begins at that moment instead of already being there.
exercises.source: Marie avait peur quand l’avion a décollé.
answers: Marie a eu peur quand l’avion a décollé.
exercises.hint: A feeling that starts is an event.
exercises.feedback: Change only the tense of avoir.
exercises.explanation: Avait peur means she was already afraid; a eu peur means she became afraid at take-off.

answers: Marie avait peur quand l’avion a décollé.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged: avait peur still says the fear was there before the plane moved.

answers: Marie avait peur quand l’avion décollait.
mistakes.why: This changes the take-off instead of the feeling, and it turns the take-off into background.

answers: Marie a été peur quand l’avion a décollé.
mistakes.why: Peur goes with avoir, not être.

answers: Marie a peur quand l’avion a décollé.
mistakes.why: A peur is the present: she is afraid now. The story is in the past.

exercises.source: avoir · je · passé composé
exercises.hint: Avoir is its own auxiliary.
exercises.feedback: The past participle of avoir is irregular.
exercises.explanation: J’ai eu, as in j’ai eu froid quand la fenêtre s’est ouverte.

mistakes.why: That is the imparfait, the tense for a state already there; the question asks for the tense of a finished event.
Été is the participle of être, not of avoir.
The participle of avoir is irregular and is not built from the infinitive.
Avoir is its own auxiliary; it does not take être.

exercises.source: Je marchais dans la rue quand, tout à coup, il ____ à pleuvoir.
exercises.hint: Tout à coup signals something sudden.
exercises.feedback: A sudden event is not background.
exercises.explanation: Tout à coup marks a sudden event, so the passé composé: il a commencé à pleuvoir.

mistakes.why: Commençait would put the rain in the background, but tout à coup announces a break in the scene: the rain starts at one precise moment.
Commence is the present, and the story is being told in the past (je marchais).

exercises.source: Au lycée, Léa rentrait tard parce qu’elle ____ à la bibliothèque chaque jour.
exercises.hint: Chaque jour points to repetition.
exercises.feedback: This happened again and again during a period.
exercises.explanation: Chaque jour marks a habit, like rentrait, so the imparfait: elle travaillait. Travaillais is the form for je or tu.

mistakes.why: That form names one finished stretch of work, but chaque jour says it was repeated day after day, like rentrait.
Travaillais carries the je/tu ending, and the subject elle takes the il/elle one.

exercises.instruction: Write manger in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Une fois, nous ____ (manger) des escargots.
exercises.hint: Une fois means one time.
exercises.feedback: A single occasion is not a habit.
exercises.explanation: Une fois marks a single occasion, so the passé composé: nous avons mangé.

mistakes.why: Mangions would make snails a habit, but une fois says it happened one single time.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, so the -s is wrong.
Manger takes avoir; sommes mangés would mean you were the ones eaten.
That is still the infinitive after the auxiliary, where the past participle belongs.

exercises.instruction: Write cuisiner in the passé composé or the imparfait.
exercises.source: Pendant que maman ____ (cuisiner), papa mettait la table.
exercises.hint: Pendant que links two actions going on at the same time.
exercises.feedback: Neither action interrupts the other.
exercises.explanation: The verb after pendant que is an ongoing action, so the imparfait: maman cuisinait.

mistakes.why: A cuisiné cuts the cooking into one finished block. After pendant que the verb is what was going on while papa set the table.
Cuisinais carries the je/tu ending, and maman is one person, il/elle.
Cuisine is the present, but mettait shows the sentence is in the past.

exercises.source: Suddenly, the door opened.
answers: Tout à coup, la porte s’est ouverte.
Tout d’un coup, la porte s’est ouverte.
exercises.hint: Suddenly marks a single sudden event. S’ouvrir takes être.
exercises.feedback: A sudden event is not background.
exercises.explanation: Soudain or tout à coup takes the passé composé: la porte s’est ouverte, with ouverte agreeing with la porte.

mistakes.why: S’ouvrait stretches the opening out as background, but soudain announces one sharp moment.
A ouvert needs someone opening something. A door that opens by itself uses s’ouvrir, which takes être in the past.
With être the participle agrees with the subject, and la porte is feminine.

exercises.instruction: Replace souvent with une fois and change the tense.
exercises.source: Nous allions souvent au cinéma.
answers: Nous sommes allés une fois au cinéma.
Nous sommes allées une fois au cinéma.
Nous sommes allés au cinéma une fois.
Nous sommes allées au cinéma une fois.
Une fois, nous sommes allés au cinéma.
Une fois, nous sommes allées au cinéma.
exercises.hint: Une fois refers to one occasion.
exercises.feedback: Change the verb as well as the time word. Aller takes être.
exercises.explanation: Une fois marks a single occasion, so the passé composé: nous sommes allés (or allées) au cinéma.

answers: Nous allions une fois au cinéma.
mistakes.why: The time word changed but the verb stayed in the habit tense, and une fois names one single visit.

answers: Nous avons allé une fois au cinéma.
mistakes.why: Aller takes être in the passé composé, never avoir.

answers: Nous sommes allé une fois au cinéma.
mistakes.why: With être the participle agrees with the subject, and nous is plural.

exercises.source: Soudain, le chat sautait sur la table.
answers: Soudain, le chat a sauté sur la table.
exercises.hint: What kind of action does soudain introduce?
exercises.feedback: Soudain does not introduce background.
exercises.explanation: Soudain marks a sudden event, so the passé composé: le chat a sauté.

answers: Soudain, le chat sautait sur la table.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence unchanged. Sautait describes the jumping as ongoing or repeated, while soudain marks one sharp moment.

answers: Soudain, le chat est sauté sur la table.
mistakes.why: Sauter takes avoir in the passé composé, not être.

answers: Tout à coup, le chat sautait sur la table.
mistakes.why: Swapping soudain for another word for suddenly changes nothing: the verb is what has to move.

exercises.source: All of a sudden, I heard a scream.
answers: Tout à coup, j’ai entendu un cri.
exercises.hint: Tout à coup introduces a sudden event.
exercises.feedback: One verb tile is in the tense for background.
exercises.explanation: Tout à coup marks a sudden event: j’ai entendu un cri.

answers: Tout à coup, j’entendais un cri.
mistakes.why: J’entendais describes hearing as something going on in the background, but tout à coup announces one sudden thing.

exercises.source: entendre · je · passé composé
exercises.hint: Entendre takes avoir, and its participle ends in -u.
exercises.feedback: Remember the elision of je before the auxiliary.
exercises.explanation: J’ai entendu, as in soudain, j’ai entendu un bruit.

mistakes.why: That is the imparfait, the background tense; the question asks for the tense of a finished event.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, so the -s is wrong.
Entendre takes avoir, not être.
Je becomes j’ in front of a vowel, with an apostrophe and no space.
